extracted.intended_audience: Metamath users, database authors, proof contributors, and maintainers (e.g., set.mm maintainers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and requirements for writing Metamath source files, definitions, proofs, typesetting metadata, and for operating the Metamath program (including mmj2 checks and set.mm conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition termination and layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must end in an unquoted semicolon; white space is not required before the terminating semicolon of a definition. Each definition should start on a new line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction may be removed in future versions of Metamath (0.177 noted), but using this form improves readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting data as quoted strings
rubrics_metrics.description: Typesetting data is a sequence of one or more quoted strings (if more than one, they are connected by +). A quoted string may use double (") or single (') quotes and may not include line breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To include a quotation mark matching the enclosing quotes, repeat it twice (e.g., "a""b" or 'c''d'). Long quoted strings can be broken into multiple quoted strings joined with +; you may use multiple lines provided a '+' is at the end of every line except the last, and the + should be preceded and followed by at least one white space character.

rubrics_metrics.name: c-style comments support
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath source supports c-style comments: /* ... */

rubrics_metrics.name: latexdef syntax and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The syntax for a LATEX definition is: latexdef "math-token" as "latex-string"; — token-string and latex-string are the data for the token and its LATEX definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These LATEX definitions are used by the Metamath program when asked to produce LATEX output using the write tex command.

rubrics_metrics.name: htmldef and althtmldef semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: HTML typesetting definitions use: htmldef "math-token" as "html-code"; and althtmldef "math-token" as "html-code"; — there are two possible definitions for math tokens in HTML to allow alternate representations (e.g., Unicode entities vs gif images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many other HTML typesetting definitions (htmltitle, htmlhome, htmlvarcolor, htmlbibliography) to control generated web pages; htmlbibliography refers to a filename that must contain <A NAME='...'> tags for bibliographic references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended HTML metadata for sections
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing multiple types of pages from a single database, declare exthtmltitle, exthtmlhome, exthtmlbibliography and exthtmllabel "label" to identify where the 'extended' section starts; during generation for that starting statement and following statements use the exthtml* values instead of html* values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to add typesetting definitions for new math tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever you add a new math token you will often want to add typesetting definitions using latexdef, htmldef, and althtmldef so they remain up to date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to use all three depends on how the database is intended to be used (e.g., LaTeX output, HTML with Unicode, or HTML with images).

rubrics_metrics.name: $j (additional information) comment syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional information comment begins with the token $j within a comment and continues until the comment close $). It contains a sequence of commands of the form: command arg arg ... ; where each arg can be a quoted string or a keyword, and every command ends in an unquoted semicolon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a verifier does not recognize a command it must skip it by finding the end-of-command semicolon. A verifier may ignore these comments entirely or only process certain commands. Systems are encouraged to coordinate on command usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of additional information commands (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional information comments can declare syntax/typecodes, register primitives, mark justifications, register equalities/definitions, declare congruence theorems, or add typecodes (e.g., syntax 'wff'; primitive 'wn' 'wi'; justification 'bijust' for 'df-bi'; equality 'wb' from ...; congruence 'notbii'; syntax 'setvar').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are example commands used in set.mm; the parser treats them like $t comments and systems may support different subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include file syntax and semantics ($[ file-name $])
rubrics_metrics.description: Use $[ file-name $] to include another Metamath source file (file-name should be a single token with same syntax as a math symbol). Comments may appear between $[ and $]. Included files may include other files recursively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All information in the included files becomes available in the including file; a drawback is that renaming symbols or labels requires updating references in including files.

rubrics_metrics.name: File naming conventions for included files
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming conventions are the same as the OS; for cross-OS compatibility keep file names simple, e.g., file.mm where 'file' is eight characters or less, in lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On older Mac OS (pre-OSX) path syntax differs; prefer simple names to avoid portability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include-file nesting and single-read behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no limit to include nesting depth; if two included files include a common third file, only the first reference to the common file will be read in (subsequent references are ignored).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this behavior you should ordinarily include common files only in the outermost block to avoid unexpected results when inner blocks try to include the same file. Self-includes are ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed proof format structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A compressed proof has overall structure: $= ( label-list ) compressed-proof $. — the initial '(' signals a compressed proof; label-list includes all statements referred to by the proof except mandatory hypotheses; compressed-proof encodes the proof using upper-case letters (think of it as a large base-26 integer); whitespace inside compressed-proof is optional and ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details are in Appendix B; the Metamath program converts between normal and compressed formats. It's best to ensure a proof is correct before compressing because severe errors in compressed proofs are less recoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of mandatory hypotheses in compressed proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of the mandatory hypotheses of the statement being proved must not be changed when using the compressed proof format, otherwise the proof will become incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you wish to change the order of mandatory hypotheses, convert the proof back to normal format first (save proof statement /normal), then reorder and possibly recompress (save proof statement /compressed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Error checking with compressed proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: During verify proof, an error found in a compressed proof may point to a character in compressed-proof which may be meaningless; in this case save proof /normal and run verify proof again to get a more meaningful error location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correctness in normal format before saving compressed proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of unknown proofs/subproofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In a proof under development, any step or subproof not yet known may be represented with a single '?', which pushes a single entry onto the RPN stack as if it were a hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All $p statements must have proofs (even if unknown). To create a completely unknown proof use: label $p statement $= ? $.; verify proof will check known portions and warn that the statement is unproved. Partially developed proofs may be saved compressed and will contain '?'s in the compressed-proof part. Use save new_proof when working with the Proof Assistant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath treats axioms and definitions uniformly ($a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic Metamath language and program make no distinction between axioms and definitions; both use the $a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although mathematicians often treat definitions as mere abbreviations, Metamath leaves concerns about 'proper' definitions to external verification tools to avoid complicating the core language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a 'proper' definition (informal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper definition should not strengthen the language and any symbols introduced by the definition should be eliminable from the language (i.e., mere typographical conveniences, theoretically superfluous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some definitions (like recursive ones) can be subtle and may require metatheorems to prove they are not creative (i.e., don't add new theorems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for direct (genuine) definitions in set.mm
rubrics_metrics.description: In set.mm the goal was to introduce almost all definitions in the form of two expressions connected by either ↔ or =, where the thing being defined does not appear on the right-hand side (a 'genuine or direct definition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct definitions are easier to eliminate mechanically and simplify the metalogic needed to justify them; recursive textbook-style definitions are instead derived as theorems from these direct definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using recursion operators to avoid metalogic
rubrics_metrics.description: set.mm defines recursion operators (rec and recs) so that operations ordinarily defined recursively (e.g., addition on ordinals, sequence generators) can be given explicit direct definitions that avoid complex metalogic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: df-rdg, df-recs, and related definitions provide machinery to convert recursive-style definitions into direct closed-form expressions; direct usage of the more primitive recs is discouraged but available when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional additional verification via mmj2 (parse check)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mmj2 verifier supports an optional parse check (SetParser command) that requires new definitions to not create an ambiguous parse for a KLR(5) parser, preventing errors such as definitions with imbalanced parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This check is enabled for set.mm continuous integration but optional for other databases; it helps ensure unambiguous grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional additional verification via mmj2 (definition soundness check)
rubrics_metrics.description: mmj2 can run a definition soundness check (definitionCheck macro) to impose additional rules for definitions (some $a statements are excluded, e.g., ax-* statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows databases (like set.mm) to require extra constraints without forcing all verifiers to implement them; the database CI enforces them for that database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition soundness rule 1: form of new definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: New definitions must be introduced using = or ↔.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition soundness rule 2: no prior use of definiendum
rubrics_metrics.description: No $a statement introduced before this one is allowed to use the symbol being defined in this definition, and the definition is not allowed to use the symbol itself (except once, in the definiendum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition soundness rule 3: variables in definiens
rubrics_metrics.description: Every variable in the definiens should not be distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent is to restrict variable distinctness declarations relative to the definiens; the verifier enforces this by analysis or requiring justification theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition soundness rule 4: dummy variable distinctness and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Every dummy variable in the definiendum is required to be distinct from each other and from variables in the definiens; to determine this the system will look for a 'justification' theorem in the database and, if not found, attempt to briefly prove (ϕ → ∀xϕ) for each dummy variable x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a justification theorem if automatic determination fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition soundness rule 5: dummy variable type
rubrics_metrics.description: Every dummy variable should be a set variable, unless there is a justification theorem available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a dummy variable is not a set variable, include a justification theorem to show it's acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition soundness rule 6: dummy variables must be bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Every dummy variable must be bound; if the system cannot determine this a justification theorem must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit binding justification theorems when binding cannot be inferred automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy: keep Metamath core simple and enforce extra rules externally
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of building constraints into the Metamath language, treat axioms and definitions uniformly and provide tools (e.g., mmj2) to verify additional conditions tailored to specific databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows optional, database-specific constraints without complicating the Metamath foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking the Metamath program
rubrics_metrics.description: On Unix: ./metamath; on Windows: metamath (from command prompt). Use command-line arguments as a list of Metamath commands (surround in quotes if they contain spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Windows surrounding quotes must be double. For Unix, any path with /s must be quoted so Metamath doesn't treat / as a command qualifier. If the command-line has one argument and no spaces, the argument is implicitly assumed to be read (special case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Command-line argument quoting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Command-line arguments that include spaces or Unix-style path separators should be quoted; in Unix use single or double quotes around the Metamath command, and within that quote file names may themselves be quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ./metamath 'read "/tmp/set.mm"'  or ./metamath '/tmp/set.mm' (the latter uses the special implicit-read case). If you get an "?Expected VERIFY" error when reading a Unix filename with slashes, you probably haven't quoted it correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command syntax and interactive behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Command lines are sequences of words separated by spaces; command words are not case sensitive and only enough letters to disambiguate are required; arguments such as file names, labels, or symbol names are case-sensitive. Use ? at the MM> prompt to list commands; pressing return selects the default choice shown in brackets. ? can be used mid-command to see choices unless a non-keyword argument is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifiers begin with a slash '/' and spaces around '/' are optional. If a command outputs more than one screenful you'll be prompted to <return> to continue, Q to quit (which completes internally but suppresses further output), or S to scroll to end; after first screen you can use 'b' to go back. Pressing ctrl-c aborts the program unconditionally and will lose unsaved work.

rubrics_metrics.name: exit/quit command behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax: exit [/force] (quit is a synonym). Exits Metamath; if there have been changes from save proof or save new_proof you will be given an opportunity to write source. In Proof Assistant mode, exit returns to MM> and may prompt to save new_proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional /force qualifier suppresses prompts and is useful in submit command files to ensure predictable behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: open log / close log usage
rubrics_metrics.description: open log file-name opens a log file that stores everything displayed on the screen; close log closes it. The log file is automatically closed upon exiting Metamath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logging to help recover from mistakes in long Proof Assistant sessions or to document bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: submit command semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax: submit filename — causes Metamath to read further command lines from the specified file. Lines beginning with '!' are comments. submit files can call submit recursively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrolling is continuous when running submit files; open a log file to record output. Optional qualifier /silent suppresses screen output but still records output in an open log file.

rubrics_metrics.name: erase command effect
rubrics_metrics.description: erase resets Metamath to its starting state, deleting any database that was read in. If there have been unsaved changes the user will be prompted to save them.

rubrics_metrics.name: set echo and set scroll commands
rubrics_metrics.description: set echo on/off causes command lines to be echoed with abbreviations expanded (useful when learning commands). set scroll prompted/continuous controls whether long listings pause or scroll continuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: set width / set height defaults and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Default screen width assumed is 79 characters and default height 24 lines; use set width number and set height number to change these values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger width helps logging proofs for wide printers; LaTeX examples in the book used 61 characters per line in typewriter font.

rubrics_metrics.name: beep and 'b' abbreviation caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: beep produces an audible beep; 'b' is an abbreviation. However, if 'b' is typed immediately after a paged display it will back up a page rather than beep — in that case type the full 'beep' command.

rubrics_metrics.name: more command and OS commands
rubrics_metrics.description: more filename displays the contents of an ASCII file. A line enclosed in single or double quotes is executed by the operating system (if it has a CLI). Trailing quote is optional. This feature is not available on Macintoshes prior to OS X.

rubrics_metrics.name: File creation and backup behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands that create new files do not overwrite an existing filename; instead the existing file is renamed filename~1, an existing filename~1 becomes filename~2, etc., up to ~9 (an existing filename~9 is deleted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes recovery easier but can clutter directories; occasionally clean up ~n files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size limitations in Metamath program
rubrics_metrics.description: In general there are no fixed, predefined limits on labels, tokens, or statements; the program uses 32-bit variables (64-bit on 64-bit CPUs) as indices and allocates arrays dynamically as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: read command behavior and /verify qualifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax: read file-name [/verify] — reads a Metamath source file and included files. Statement syntax is checked during read, but proof syntax is not checked unless /verify is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The /verify qualifier will verify all proofs as the database is read (slows reading). File names may be quoted; if prompted for the file name do not put quotes around it.

rubrics_metrics.name: verify_proof troubleshooting for compressed proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When verify proof reports an error in compressed format pointing to a character in compressed-proof, convert to normal format (save proof /normal) and re-run verify proof to get a more meaningful error location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compressed proofs are efficient but less transparent for debugging; prefer verifying and debugging in normal format before compressing.
